results.reason: The ledger exists with 1,901 required outcome rows, owners for WP-00 through WP-32 and references to all 55 gap IDs. An independent read-only inventory comparison found references for all 1,314 distinct roadmap file paths, 192 task strings, and 70 checklist strings. These reference matches do not establish the required one-row-per-observable-variant inventory: for example G04 combines request propagation, cache partitioning and subscriber cancellation in one row, with options and backends left empty. Of 1,901 rows, 1,899 have empty backend arrays. Thus complete enumeration of format variants, options and backends remains unsupported.

Rows record IDs, priority, owner, desired behavior and source/acceptance status, but the required category and root/package/internal exposure are not present as per-row fields, and source mappings and evidence are largely empty. The G01 row gives a concrete example: files, symbols and public entrypoints are empty, the test is an owner-triage placeholder and evidence is empty. Across the ledger 1,896 rows lack symbols, 1,897 lack public entrypoints, and all 1,901 have empty source-evidence arrays; generic limitations do not establish device/backend limits.

An earlier assessment inspected a sample of 198 of 1,901 outcomes, and the current ledger marks 1,878 outcomes unverified. The sample explicitly describes mixed-time, non-immutable observations. The ledger retains unverified rows without public entrypoint, source path or evidence, such as G01; a completed exhaustive recheck against source, exports, installed packages and relevant tests and a semantic merge are not demonstrated. No test proves that exhaustive recheck occurred.

The ledger assigns owners and tracks planning and acceptance state; its checkpoint does not claim global CODE_COMPLETE_GO, and the source gate requires implemented, complete, owned rows and matching checks. However, exact file actions and acceptance criteria are not recorded for every named capability: the G01 row has no implementation files and its required test remains an owner-triage placeholder. Discovery and correct breakdown of every newly found option is not established, so this is not complete even though the no-false-completion guard exists.

The ledger distinguishes source from not-run acceptance and records a generic limitation, avoiding a fabricated device pass. It does not provide the required per-capability package/subpath, backend, version, format, browser/OS/device or distinct evidence-level cells: 1,897 of 1,901 rows have empty public-entrypoint arrays, 1,899 have empty backend arrays and no row records retained source evidence. Physical-device evidence is correctly deferred acceptance; the missing matrix structure and population are source-ledger work.

The specified WP-00 ledger exists and records outcome IDs, owners, statuses, generic limitations and some file or test references. It does not record the required API, implementation, tests, specific limitations and retained evidence for each capability; the G01 row has empty files, symbols, public entrypoints and evidence and its source test is an unresolved triage instruction. The current source ledger test checks structure, not actual behavioral proof.

The ledger maps 1,901 required outcomes to work-package owners, including the G26 row. It does not close the public capability/option inventory with executable evidence: only four rows have public entrypoints, no row has retained source evidence, and its checkpoint records zero completed source outcomes. These ledger facts are not a claim that zero product implementations exist. A source-only ledger contract test exists, but it does not establish every public option or execute every required check.

Some public options reach downstream consumers and the source option probes include an actionable unsupported plane parameter, but the universal behavior contract is not met. AuraCameraSpec publicly types roll and camera.perspective accepts that type, yet its returned object does not copy roll or raise an error; the diagnostic registry describes camera.roll as having no runtime consumer. The root engine exports camera. Existing option-discovery probes are restricted to a named set of builder namespaces and source observations, so they cannot establish the universal visual/hardware requirement. Actual visual/device acceptance is deferred, and no rendered claim follows from the source evidence.

Bounds remain the default; triangle mesh queries compose transforms and handle live morph/skin/instances, filtering, ordered ties, absent geometry, degenerates and disposal. Non-triangle topology yields no mesh hits; arbitrary vertex-shader deformation is not evaluated.
Custom indexed geometry is validated and compiled into an index buffer; indexed triangle intersections use that buffer. An empty index list is deliberately non-indexed.
Analytic two-bone and pose-rotation solvers are exported and consumed by the actor constraint path; zero segment length and coincident root/target are rejected.
Integer typed custom streams support normalized conversion, stride and offset; normalized float data is explicitly rejected and supported GPU-incompatible layouts use a float fallback.

Live triangle intersections cover skinning, morphs, instances, UV/barycentrics and filters, but SceneQueries walks every triangle directly instead of integrating the separately exported BVH; arbitrary custom vertex shaders are not evaluated.

All grouped source requirements are evidenced: origin-default queries, disposed batches and typed stream decoding; independent point-form transform/scene-graph expectations; tangent-without-normal texture packing with bounds and fixed shader slots; and literal packed-data tests across normal/tangent combinations, vertices, layers and formats. No tests were executed.

Public geometry exports typed layouts, normalized/interleaved streams, safe operations and runtime attribute updates through handles. Supported custom stream names and formats are validated; invalid layouts are rejected.

Triangle ray queries return exact geometric intersections and are publicly exported, but the query evaluates CPU position, morph and skin streams rather than arbitrary custom vertex shader deformation; non-triangle geometry returns no mesh hits.
Position edits clear authored bounds and recompute live culling bounds. An installed-app visual regression exists, but its visible-moving-geometry assertion is deferred and not claimed as passed.
Public batched state is rendered and queried with per-slot transforms and identities, including disposal. Slots may be reused after deletion and are not unique lifetime tokens.
CLI GLB optimization can apply meshopt compression and asset loaders accept injected Draco/meshopt decoders. A general public runtime geometry compression encoder/helper is not established.

Compiler builds normalized custom attribute layouts and syncs live mutations, refreshing bounds after position changes. Unsupported GPU layouts fall back to float storage; changing the footprint rebuilds geometry.
Position attribute edits remove old authored bounds and the live geometry resource refreshes from all positions; other attribute changes do not trigger that position refresh.
Render bounds calculate weighted morphs and skinning, with per-joint culling bounds and instance transforms; arbitrary custom shader displacement is outside these CPU calculations.

Parent transforms, origin nodes, bounds and triangle mesh queries plus submitted-item cache synchronization are present. Triangle traversal does not evaluate custom vertex shader deformation, and a batch slot can be recycled for a later member.
CCD iterative IK is wired into the actor animation path. The solver caps iterations at eight and returns reached:false for unreachable targets.
Public toNonIndexed expands built-in, custom and morph channels in index order, retaining groups and draw ranges, and rejects incomplete primitives or unsupported streams.
Affine transforms use inverse-transpose normals; merge/deindex preserve supported streams and metadata or reject unsupported fields and incompatible topology, morphs and draw ranges.

Runtime handles compute live primitive geometry bounds, but model bounds can use declared asset metadata, so general bounds cannot be claimed exact for every animated or custom-shader-deformed object.
Merge and deindex validate unknown top-level streams, expand supported custom and morph streams, preserve groups and topology, and reject mismatched streams and unrepresentable draw ranges.
Public updateAttribute accepts a range, synchronizes it to live vertex storage and marks dirty bytes. Overruns and unsupported attributes are rejected.
Picking evaluates current morph targets and skin palettes, but cannot reproduce arbitrary custom vertex shader deformation; non-triangle geometry is also a miss.
Supported attribute and morph streams are preserved through deindex and merge; unknown streams, inconsistent layouts and unrepresentable draw ranges fail explicitly.
Code clears old position bounds and refreshes live geometry bounds; the browser test for rendered movement exists but has not been run and is acceptance evidence.
Mesh picking implements live transforms, instances, position morphs, skin palettes, UV/face output, sides and stable ordering; custom vertex shader displacement is not evaluated by the CPU query.

Skeleton, morph controls, two-bone/CCD solvers, animation bounds and disposal paths exist, but a complete audit of every facial-control, procedural pose and lifetime variant is not established from these paths alone.
Skeleton validates parent order and composes world matrices with inverse-bind matrices. Invalid parent indices fail explicitly.

Runtime position edits clear stale bounds and query state exposes live geometry, transforms, morphs and submitted items. Empty indices mean sequential non-indexed geometry; mesh queries use sequential vertices and dynamic geometry may synthesize safe indices. Incomplete primitives are rejected during geometry operations.
Index width changes at a maximum index of 65,536; generated sequential indices cover all three named boundary counts. Tests exist and were not executed.

The renderer has forward/clustered and three distinct native paths, but render bundles have only a prototype screen and no backend call sites; the alternate paths also reject or fall back for multiple views, shadows, some lights and transparent/instanced input.

The explicit opt-in routes to a native backend and retains its experimental support label. Rendered output, dispatch, repeated lifecycle and separate software/hardware results are acceptance evidence, deferred until code freeze; tests existing are not a current pass.

Root initialization selects a native device and renderer; native source submission, materials, textures, shadows and presentation are present. Deferred, meshlet and visibility are independently selected, with explicit fallback for unsupported scenes or capabilities; source tests have not been run.

Bounded meshlet construction and compute culling drive indirect native draws; missing compute or exceeded limits produce an explicit failure or permitted forward fallback. The root renderer selects it only for admitted frames.
Backend selection awaits device and renderer initialization and checks native rendering/canvas capabilities. An unavailable device fails or follows the explicit fallback policy.

Deferred capability negotiation, supported native G-buffer/resolve, trusted feature admission, borrowed probe/surface leases, and depth-copy shader are present. The grouped requirement for native-drawing-output-integration.test.ts remains incomplete: that file tests feature admission and flag derivation only, not the stated drawing output, resource ownership, sorting and explicit fallback. Other named tests cover parts of those contracts; none was run. Unsupported scene features require explicit forward fallback or failure.
Root diagnostics expose requested and active backend, missing features, fallback reason and drawing-path diagnostics; failures use explicit capability errors.
Device initialization validates requested WebGPU features and limits and emits named errors; explicit webgpu fails unless allowFallback is true, while choosing auto authorizes fallback.
Required adapter features and limits are validated and named errors identify unavailable capabilities; initialization also checks native pipeline support.

Unsupported drawing features are either rejected before submission or forwarded to the complete forward route if explicitly allowed, with a diagnostic reason; failed backend initialization follows its separate permission flag.

Generation-scoped leases and queue fencing exist for shared native resources, but the broad target-sharing contract for color/depth, cube/array/3D layers, multisampling, copy and readback across all combinations was not fully established here; multisampled depth resolve is explicitly unsupported.
Root and native backend disposal release renderer and scene resources; device-owned resource interop waits for queue completion or invalidation, while borrowed ownership is preserved.
The root resolves backend intent, asynchronously creates and validates the actual renderer, honors allowFallback, and reports active backend and fallback reason.

Native draw-state mapping and scene render precompile exist, including target/layout/device keys. A corresponding compute-variant warmup without presentation was not established; the simple WebGPU pipeline cache only provides get/create and clear.

Initialization checks actual native capabilities and app compute shares the selected device and queue. Full same-scene, unchanged provenance and material behavior across both backends is not established for all inputs; the native device explicitly rejects several vertex-format conversions.

The device tracks sampled-texture policy and vertex-conversion budgets and reports limit errors. A complete GPU memory-budget policy and precise diagnostics for every unsupported feature were not established.

Visibility rasterization stores primitive IDs and normals and performs per-triangle material resolve; device attachment and storage limits produce explicit failure or allowed forward fallback. It is restricted to admitted opaque scenes.
Root app accepts webgpu or the experimental-webgpu profile and initializes a native GPU renderer; WebGL2 remains the default and auto is explicit opt-in.

Interop validates per-generation leases, submits compute and render in queue order, and fence-retires resources. WebGPU performs inter-pass transitions; the API does not expose manual barriers. Foreign resources and conflicting access are rejected.
RenderBackend forwards required features and limits to WebGPUDevice; after device creation, failed owned initialization destroys the device while injected borrowed devices are retained.
Render-bundle source is an evaluation screen only; the parity plan explicitly reports zero engine backend renderBundle call sites.

A source test suite covers simulated native deferred, visibility, meshlet construction and culling, fallbacks, unsupported materials and allocation/lifecycle behavior; this inspection does not establish a current pass.

The root profile remains experimental and routes explicit WebGPU requests instead of unconditionally rejecting them. Actual native output, dispatch, repeated lifecycle and separate software/hardware records are deferred acceptance evidence.
Forward rendering sorts collected items, while the public WebGPU subpath exports a bounded stable GPU sorter. Alternate opaque paths reject transparent objects or explicitly fall back to forward.

Root app binds compute to its selected renderer device and generation; the shared queue interop validates ownership and synchronization. The grouped regression test exercises same native buffer/texture leases, foreign-device and usage rejection, generation replacement and a root compute-to-material buffer. Tests were inspected but not run.

A browser test renders a small authored scene through the three direct pipeline classes and checks pixels and adapter diagnostics, but it is not evidence of a current run, does not exercise root backend selection, and skips when no adapter is available. Acceptance is deferred until code freeze.
Generation-owned leases prohibit cross-device resources and retain retired handles until queue fence completion or device loss; app and backend disposal retire owners.

Native feature negotiation, ownership, recovery, full state mapping and multiple vertex streams exist, but small-integer conversions and three-component vertex formats are explicitly unsupported; the entire broad buffer-layout/color/texture contract was not proven.
App compute follows selected device and generation, submits through shared resource interop, and disposes prior contexts on replacement; loss and recreation have source tests but no current pass.
Construction enforces vertex/triangle bounds, GPU culling writes indirect work, and workgroups/draws/buffer sizes are limited before submission with strict failure or permitted fallback.

Functional explicit WebGPU opt-in replaces unconditional rejection and its root quality profile stays experimental. Source tests and rendered acceptance are tracked separately; supported/default promotion is deferred.

A bounded GPU sort, compute/render shared queue, indirect meshlet draws and async readback exist, with several explicit failures. A complete query and device-wide memory budget contract and diagnostics for all unsupported cases were not established.
A distinct visibility geometry pass records primitive IDs then resolves material and normals, with explicit attachment/storage capability limits and allowed forward fallback.
Root compute automatically binds to the mounted renderer native device, queue and generation and retires the previous context on selection changes; foreign device bindings are rejected.
App-bound compute and rendering share device-owned buffer/texture leases and a queue; conflicting accesses, foreign resources, missing usages and stale generations are rejected.

WebGL restoration remounts the scene, and WebGPU loss disposes compute and schedules one renderer remount; the device-level recover operation requests a replacement device. Injected devices require replacement by their owner.

Native render-state resolution and render precompile have target/layout/device identity and cancellation-related tests, but compute-variant warmup was not established; full cross-package typed buffer layout consumption and every listed test contract remain unproven.

Environment cache and probe paths deliver environment illumination and local reflection support; individual environment combinations remain bounded.

Root emissive material and generated PBR emissive factor/map contribution exist; specific backend limits remain as declared by material validation.

Incremental lightmap output and caller-owned root attachment feed a validated draw consumer with explicit UV and composition policy.
Reflection probe capture and box projection have authored node and renderer paths; supported sizes/update modes are bounded.
Diffuse transmission lobe and sampled-map WGSL code exist, but full supported-lobe combinations and independent shader replacement are not established.
Rough diffuse has a mapped scalar texture path and UV transforms, but backend combinations and UV channel limits are constrained and independent physical shader completion remains open.
A bounded public retroreflection scalar feeds the direct diffuse BRDF in both shader paths.
Clustered lighting, grids, CPU fallback voxels and cascades exist, but clustered photometric/projected lights explicitly reject indexing and no broad cross-backend correctness result is established.
Multiple light kinds, cascades, probes and bounded CPU voxel baking exist; clustered profiles and projected WebGPU/clustered draws are unsupported, so the aggregate is incomplete.
Material types expose opaque, mask, blend and alpha-to-coverage; generated shader has explicit target/coverage validation.
Public physical spec resolves rough diffuse, retroreflection and iridescence min/max with legacy tuple compatibility; the renderer has both language formulas.
Profiled direct lights, projected spot, cluster/probe and cascaded paths exist, but profile/projection cluster indexing and WebGPU projected images are explicitly unsupported.
Incremental bake consumes generated atlas destination, chart bounds, gutters and texel density; cancellation and result ownership are explicit. CPU implementation and finite work limits apply.
Type-C IES parsing and non-clustered point/spot admission exist, but external tilt files and Type-A/B are unsupported and profiled cluster indexing is not implemented.
Per-lobe textures, UV transforms and tangent hooks are present, but extension matrix explicitly marks several lobes bounded and full authored tangent identity remains open.
Caller-owned probe grids, voxel data and lightmaps attach through app-owned advanced-lighting state, with renderer consumption subject to finite binding limits.
Grid implements bounds, per-backend budgets, SH updates, interpolation/evaluation and uploadable render data; a compatible consumer or explicit app attachment is required.

Both-backend authored browser scene exists, but current pixel execution and required backend availability were not established; deferred to acceptance.
Atlas shader source exists and uses documented approximations, but this audit did not establish a complete provenance review or replacement of every adapted implementation.

Photometry, orientation, shadow visibility, min/max and invalid-input tests exist, while lobe-energy tests are in a separate shader test; the specified physical-lighting file alone does not cover energy.
Punctual shader and independent CPU mirror implementations exist, but full provenance review and necessity of replacement for both files is not established by source text alone.
Root point light builder and physical collected-light conversion exist; shadow and profile cases have their own stated limits.
Transmission and scene-color capture exist, but the support matrix explicitly reports a bounded pass and missing backdrop fallback.
Embedded neutral, optional preset errors and generated lookup numerical tests exist, but full notice-retention disposition across all unreplaced attributed shaders was not established.

The browser source renders updated probe and voxel-derived bakes, but it skips unavailable backends and no current visible-result receipt was supplied. Its consumer does not claim real-time GPU voxel tracing.
Root material.custom validates GLSL custom material and allows a WGSL counterpart; portable package material provides paired backend support. WGSL-only custom source is not accepted.
Rough diffuse, retroreflection and film endpoints are wired, but layered extension support remains bounded and independent WGSL preview excludes combinations.

The independently documented BRDF chunk implements bounded rough diffuse and layered energy redistribution; shader reference tests cover energy and reciprocity. This does not establish replacement of all other lobes.
The matrix reports UV, texture limits and backend-specific fallbacks, but full supported physical combinations remain bounded and independent WebGPU preview rejects combinations.
Layered clearcoat exists but support matrix bounds multiple scattering; the independent WGSL replacement is only an opt-in source preview.
The bounded SH9 probe grid interpolates, updates and produces renderer data; use requires a consuming renderer or app attachment.
A three-band dispersion shader and generated WebGPU variant exist, but dispersion is conditional on transmission and complete supported combinations are not established.
Photometric tests cover rotational and 2D/angular symmetry, linear factors and malformed tables; generated atlas bake tests check chart/gutter metadata and preservation of authored UV.
Directional shadow options and runtime compile 1–4 cascades with tier-dependent limits and generated shader metadata.

Graph IR validates and generates GLSL/WGSL and rejects unsupported compute/storage on WebGL2; tests inspect generated strings, but comprehensive validation by actual backend shader compilers for every supported variant is not established.
Root ambient node is collected by the authored lighting path; legacy and physical flag routes have different defaults.
Environment probe build, cache and prefilter paths exist, but the WebGPU generated path restricts environment variants and no complete backend-wide prefilter result is established.
Root PBR and physical factories exist and generated PBR includes many lobe features; full physical combinations and independent shader replacement remain bounded.
Root spot builder supports color, cone, power, range, profile and projection; modulation and shadow paths have separate explicit limits.
Legacy TSL supports typed local variables, while persistent cross-backend graph locals are loop indices rather than general mutable graph variables.
The public depth factory makes depth24 and the GL upload path handles depth; standalone depth texture upload is rejected on native WebGPU, and depth target capability is restricted.
Texture handles carry min/mag filters into samplers; float32 filtering is capability-gated.
Base color is exposed as color and texture with UV selection and reaches material bindings.

All four grouped deliverables are present: sort tests assert stable ordering, limits and fenced cleanup; resource-limit tests assert WebGPU and linked-active WebGL sampler budgets; storage-layout tests assert bindings, stage access and borrowed-resource lifetime; the contact note documents certification, raw reload invalidation and graph rebuild. These are mock/source tests, not a current pass or evidence of rendered contact pixels; the note records that the production prepass still rejects portable graph participants.
The public dataArray factory validates data and creates a 2D-array texture; native devices include array upload/view paths. Supported formats are bounded.
Factories and mip validation exist, but WebGPU rejects layered render targets and lacks the generic target transfer methods, 3D render targets are not expressible, and splats still sort on CPU.
Compute read allocates a staging buffer per call, copies the mapped result and destroys staging; disposal cancellation has a unit test.
Target hazard checks and same-device compute interop exist; generic target transfer and cancellation contracts are not implemented on the WebGPU device.
The typed graph IR provides if/loop statements, but validation explicitly forbids those compute statements in material graphs.
Typed graphs sample color 2D and 3D textures and load depth; unsupported sampler kinds remain explicitly outside the IR.
Factories and mip validation exist, but WebGPU rejects layered render targets and lacks the generic target transfer methods, 3D render targets are not expressible, and splats still sort on CPU.
Both device paths allocate multisampled targets and resolve color, with capability checks; WebGPU permits sample counts 1 or 4 and cannot resolve depth textures.
Physical material exposes roughness and a map; graph material also has a roughness output.
Shader data layouts derive nested struct alignment and offsets and write each field with typed values; WGSL host bool is rejected.
Factories, samplers and uploads exist, but standalone depth cannot upload on native WebGPU, compressed 3D is rejected and generic target readback is not available on the WebGPU RenderDevice.
Dynamic geometry carries topology, groups and morphs, chooses wider indices as needed, and refreshes bounds after position updates; transforms use inverse-transpose normals.
Material surface exposes occlusion map and strength and compiles the core texture binding.
WebGL and mock implement the generic async color resolve; WebGPU resolves as part of render pass but does not implement the optional generic resolveRenderTarget method.
DataView writes signed, unsigned, boolean and float components to separate byte encodings; std140 and WGSL layouts have different constraints.
WebGL and mock expose generic color/depth copy; WebGPU only exposes a narrower color-region copy and lacks the generic async copy method.
The interface declares attachment identity, optional transfers and disposal, but 3D targets are absent and WebGPU does not implement its generic copy/resolve/readback methods.

Typed graph validation, stable serialization and material outputs exist internally and material.node reaches them, but the shaderGraph serialization/compile facade is absent from published engine exports; WebGL compute/storage fail closed.

Target-aware layout and DataView typed writes validate scalar, vector, matrix, array and struct values; WGSL bool storage is correctly rejected as non-host-shareable.
WebGL supports cube and 2D-array target layers; the common target descriptor has no 3D mode and WebGPU rejects layered targets.
ShaderDataLayout derives target-specific offsets and typed writes, but the graph IR has only scalar/vector value types and does not supply array/struct graph schemas to this layout engine.

Typed IR, validation, control flow and paired material shader generation exist; engine public entries omit the graph serialization facade and GLSL compute is explicitly unsupported.

Material and compute graphs generate backend-specific code with texture/storage support, but the engine public graph facade is absent, and flow control cannot be used in material graphs.

Typed IR, validation, control flow and paired material shader generation exist; engine public entries omit the graph serialization facade and GLSL compute is explicitly unsupported. MaterialBinding separately validates unsigned scalar range against the portable schema.

Mutable handle wrapS/wrapT options become sampler addresses; modes are bounded by supported enums.

The native GPU pipeline key includes resource generations, attachments, layouts and fixed state, and program keys normalize structural features; the forward program path does not select logarithmic-depth from the active convention and target generation is not itself part of ProgramKey.

Stable sorting and a bounded weighted pass with sorted fallback exist, but masked items enter the opaque forward bucket and weighted rendering rejects WebGPU and renderer multi-view. MSAA, transmission and non-alpha states fall back to sorted rendering.

Structural features and uniform values are separated, and feature keys are canonical, but active logarithmic-depth state is not selected in the forward program path. Source tests cover selected variants and reuse, not every shader-affecting state and ordinary uniform edit.

Native draw commands implement extensive state on both devices, but the material-facing state type omits winding, sample mask, blend constant and attachment overrides; WebGL2 rejects partial sample masks and offset clamp, and generated WebGPU alpha-to-coverage is unsupported.

ProgramFeatures represents material, geometry-derived and target language axes plus clipping/log-depth bits, and forward selection includes clipping and geometry. Active forward logarithmic depth is not selected by the renderer/warmup path; generated variants reject some graph and weighted combinations.

Content keys encode complete stream layouts and current vertex/index bytes with hashes and bytewise collision checks. Tests cover byte edits and distinct stream/layout identity; unsupported batching layouts remain pass-through.

Buffers and stream layouts reach both native draws and source tests inspect real bytes. Browser pixel fixture checks a normalized instance stream but has no integer shader-input pixel case; browser acceptance has not run. WebGPU divisors above one are rejected.

The bounded weighted pass documents that it approximates intersecting surfaces and is not refraction or exact ordering; eligible renderer inputs invoke accumulation and revealage. It is restricted to WebGL2/mock, and WebGPU or ineligible states use sorted fallback.

A browser specification declares both backends and pixel assertions for the listed state and normalized instance data; unsupported backends are skipped, and integer shader-input pixels are not covered. No browser execution or pixel result was established.

The sorting helper ranks opaque, transmission, mask and transparent with explicit renderOrder and stable ties, but the actual forward mapping creates only opaque, transmission and transparent buckets, so masked materials do not get a distinct mask bucket.

The draw-item contract carries temporal identity, previous transforms/joints/morphs, and per-item global/material clipping snapshots. Specialized rendering paths can reject clipping or deformation; those limits are outside the data contract itself.

The pass resolves premultiplied output and composites accumulated color and revealage over scene color; tests specify premultiplied equivalence. Refractive, custom blend and weighted MSAA cases fall back to sorted rendering.

Browser specification covers submission order, opaque occlusion, premultiplied alpha, MSAA fallback, views, teardown and transmission fallback; it was not run and uses hand-written WebGPU weighted shaders while generated WGSL weighted rendering is unsupported. Refraction remains a separate bounded path.

ForwardPass selects clipping, carries material render state to a pipeline and sorts draws, but Material.RenderState omits several DrawCommand state fields and the actual forward sort has no distinct mask bucket; logarithmic-depth feature selection is not established.

Direct device commands map many requested fields, but the public material state does not expose winding, blend constant, sample mask or independent attachment state; WebGL2 rejects partial masks and offset clamp and WebGPU generated alpha-to-coverage is rejected.

The pool copies exact vertex bytes and requires matching layouts. Unsupported multiple streams, instance-step streams, topology and indexing are explicitly rejected; the planner routes unsupported layouts around batching.

Native typed streams and many device-state/cache fields are present, but Material.RenderState does not expose all command fields, WebGL2 rejects partial sample masks/clamps, and forward logarithmic-depth feature selection is incomplete. Integer shader-input pixel evidence is also absent.

The standalone pass implements approximation, composition, opaque depth and keyed per-view allocations with sorted fallback; public renderer weighted rendering is limited to WebGL2/mock and excludes multi-view, while WGSL generation explicitly throws.

ProgramKey serializes normalized structural features, ProgramCache is per-device and invalidates generations, and native pipeline keys include target/device generation. ProgramKey itself contains no target generation, and forward logarithmic-depth feature selection is not established.

WebGPU distinguishes dynamic scissor/blend constant/stencil reference from fixed pipeline state, whose canonical identity includes target/device generations, shader/layout, vertex layouts and attachments. Unsupported attachment formats, limits and invalid combinations reject before submission.

Generator incorporates graph outputs, clipping/log-depth/output features and live physical map UVs, with strict error paths. Forward selection does not derive logarithmic depth; graph alpha-test/depth and weighted WGSL are explicitly unsupported, so complete dependencies across paths are not established.

The weighted pass binds sampled opaque depth to accumulation and revealage shaders; the renderer requires a matching sampleable depth texture. MSAA and logarithmic depth fall back; actual device-pixel evidence was not run.

The WebGPU pipeline key and dynamic-state split are wired to submission, and WebGL2 applies state per draw; however Material.RenderState cannot express all richer command fields, WebGL2 rejects partial sample masks/clamp, and generated WebGPU alpha-to-coverage is rejected.

A browser specification draws permuted layers, compares pixels, tests opaque depth, transmission/MSAA fallback, isolated views and disposal; it may skip unavailable backends and uses a fixture-supplied WebGPU weighted shader. The browser specification was not executed.

Static planning keys the full render-state signature and includes shaderVariant, but explicitly refuses graph/variant materials because synthesized batch materials do not carry their identity. Graph identity therefore is not carried through merged draws.

Shared blend contract defines named/custom color and alpha factors/equations and depth comparisons, with validation; both device paths consume it. Illegal saturated factors and backend-specific unsupported state reject explicitly.

A public bounded transmission/refraction path and material parameters exist, with separate renderer capture planning; documented limitations include missing depth ray marching and physical caustic projection, not full refraction parity.

NativeRenderState maps supported render and attachment fields to fixed pipeline state, dynamic scissor/blend constant/stencil reference and a deterministic target/layout/shader/device key; WebGPU draw uses the result. Unsupported formats, sample counts and bias combinations fail explicitly.

Native device submission resolves state and keys pipelines, and validates many invalid combinations, but Material.RenderState exposes fewer fields than RenderCommandState, leaving winding, sample mask, blend constant and attachment overrides unavailable through the material API.

The standalone pass executes bounded accumulation/revealage with sampled opaque depth, alpha composition, keyed per-view lifetime and explicit sorted fallback. Weighted MSAA, logarithmic depth and unsupported formats fall back; renderer integration is WebGL2/mock only.

Material validation preserves the existing rejection of blended depth writes and checks a few fields; it does not call the complete shared command-state validator or expose all backend requirements. A new explicit blended-depth-write policy exists only on RenderCommandState.

VertexFormat models typed/normalized/integer storage, byte alignment, separate slots, instance steps and divisors. Invalid combinations reject; WebGPU supports only divisor one and rejects or converts some device-specific formats.

Public video polling, canvas and subregion updates exist with retained storage and borrowed-source cleanup, but compressed fallback updates are rejected and 3D region edits are restricted to whole mips; external-frame lifetime validation is not established.

Known-vector/HDR source assertions and browser pixel, isolation, block-length, changing-media and cleanup specifications exist; browser verification is deferred and the source test does not establish explicit invalid external-frame lifetime validation across supported backends.

Production conversion normalizes legacy linear to linear-sRGB and delegates all declared spaces to the shared managed converter, which rejects unknown spaces. Native shader and BC1 tests exist; those test files are not evidence of a current pass.

OutputPass validates and negotiates canvas color, keys its tone/gamut/transfer shader by active output and explicit alpha, and rejects unsupported render-target P3 or unverified alpha. WebGPU only permits opaque or premultiplied presentation.
Float HDR intermediates and HDR-preserving transforms are implemented, with rgba8 fallback; an HDR physical-display swapchain is expressly unexposed and remains unverified.
Managed conversion, app policy, negotiation and dynamic uploads are wired, but public renderer diagnostics retain a fixed sRGB label and compressed fallback updates and 3D subregions are unsupported.

WebGL and WebGPU negotiate and verify requested P3 and fall back to sRGB, but WebGPU rejects P3 with non-opaque alpha even where the context might otherwise support it; incompatible post chains also reject output policy.

Color conversion, negotiated presentation and retained texture edits are present; public renderer diagnostics still hard-code sRGB, 3D subregions are whole-mip only, and compressed fallback revisions are rejected.

Dispose drops the borrowed image/canvas/video reference, polling callback and pixel references, notifies device owners, and compiler-owned bitmaps are explicitly closed. Borrowed sources remain the caller’s responsibility.

The post graph exposes and executes an output stage and device-level clear operations exist, but the cited public post graph does not establish separate texture and save stages as required by the checklist.

An extended-range managed API separates transfer, primary conversion and exposure/tone/gamut output stages; the older clamping helpers are retained separately. Output policy supports only the explicitly declared operators/spaces.

The named tests cover storage identity, orientation/unpack restoration, arrays, mips, bounds and disposal; they use mock polling and do not test validity/lifetime errors for external VideoFrame objects before upload.
The devices negotiate P3 with sRGB fallback, but WebGPU restricts P3 to opaque unorm and public renderer diagnostics hard-code sRGB instead of the negotiated value.

Low-level report separates active/fallback, float intermediates and unverified HDR display, and data maps require linear bindings; public renderer diagnostics still report a fixed sRGB label for P3 apps.

Typed byte staging implements GLSL std140/std430 and WGSL uniform/storage layout, integers, padding and matrix strides; WGSL bool is intentionally rejected in favor of u32. Tests assert exact bytes and mock uploaded data, but GPU uploaded/read-back mixed-field values are not established.
The public managed converter preserves negative and above-one finite scene-linear values and derives P3/sRGB primary transforms; its old normalized conversion remains intentionally clamped.
Upload restores WebGL unpack state and updates isolated layers/full mips using retained storage, but compressed fallback revisions are explicitly rejected and 3D partial-region edits are unavailable.

The public video factory borrows an image source and polls readyState/currentTime per bind, preserving color tagging and flip with disposal removing polling. It is a video-element cadence contract; independent VideoFrame lifetime/ownership is not established.

Borrowed-source ownership, polling, dimensions, orientation, revision, storage replacement and full compressed-mip length validation are present, but no pre-upload closed external-frame check or alpha-mode source contract is established; 3D and compressed subregions are unsupported.

The named source test contains independent primaries, negative/HDR identity and transfer round trips, alpha association, data-map and invalid-input assertions. It is a source test, not a current pass.
The rendering visual report includes requested/active/fallback and unverified physical HDR, but public renderer diagnostics and types hard-code the output label to sRGB even for a negotiated P3 app.

A packed-candidate browser specification covers pixels, resizing, layers/mips, app isolation and cleanup for WebGL2/WebGPU, with BC1 cube scoped to WebGL2; the required browser acceptance was not run.

UniformBlock optionally tracks byte differences, coalesces to four-byte-aligned partial updates and invalidates on lifecycle/failure; default uploads are full and tracked mode assumes exclusive writes.

The visual pipeline report correctly separates negotiated P3, fallback, float intermediates and unverified physical HDR, while the public app renderer report still exposes a hard-coded sRGB active label.

The shared managed converter separates transfer/primaries and scene-to-display stages, derives primaries from chromaticities and preserves finite extended range. It supports sRGB and P3 families, not Rec.2020.
Per-app sRGB/opaque defaults and validation are forwarded at renderer creation; runtime setOutput warns and is ignored on a direct output path, and changing canvas alpha after creation is rejected.
Generated RGBA8 source/data mipmaps and explicit full-mip replacement exist, but automatic data-mip generation is limited to rgba8; region edits cannot select an arbitrary mip or 3D subvolume.
Video polling, canvas revision uploads and 2D/array rectangles are implemented, but 3D edits are whole-mip only and compressed fallback updates are rejected.
A frozen packed-consumer browser spec reads pixels through a textured lit postprocessed app and checks negotiated P3 or fallback, but it is WebGL2-only and has not been run for the current candidate.
Negotiation and low-level diagnostics exist and PBR data bindings require linear color, but public renderer diagnostics hard-code sRGB and WebGPU only offers P3 for opaque unorm canvases.
The public canvas texture provides manual dirty updates, source color/flip metadata, resize handling and borrowed-source cleanup; unsupported source readback/capabilities remain backend-dependent.

Borrowed lifetime, flip, color-space, dynamic dimensions and storage reuse/reallocation are implemented, but explicit closed external-frame validation and WebGPU VideoFrame display-dimension support are not established.

Public data and array factories validate formats and dimensions; rendering textures implement bounded 2D/array updates with retained bytes. Compressed, depth and 3D region updates are explicitly outside this update method.
Video/canvas changes, 2D-array rectangles and isolated full mip updates are implemented; 3D subregions and compressed fallback revisions are rejected.
Managed HDR conversion, texture semantics and negotiated output exist, but public renderer diagnostics still report sRGB unconditionally and texture input tags are limited to linear/sRGB.

The managed converter supports sRGB/P3 primaries, extended values and data map semantics; report separates float from unverified physical HDR. The public app renderer diagnostic still hard-codes sRGB after a P3 negotiation.

Output negotiation, 3D formats and dimension-specific bind paths exist, but the WebGL sampler cache keys 2D and 3D identically; a previously created 2D sampler may be reused for 3D without setting WRAP_R. This is source inference, not a test failure.

Data-map semantics are identity-converted and PBR normal/metallic-roughness/occlusion bindings require linear texture data. Output alpha is explicitly validated and unverified canvas associations are rejected; WebGPU does not expose straight canvas alpha.

sRGB/linear texture tags, sRGB GPU storage and linear data bindings are implemented, but P3 texture-input tagging is not represented and public app diagnostics still unconditionally report sRGB output.
